planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into lean, fast-draining ground; this landrace is traditionally grown dry-farmed without irrigation, so established plants should be watered sparingly to concentrate flavor.

directions: Santorini's small, ribbed cherry tomato carries European PDO status and is traditionally dry-farmed in the island's porous volcanic ash, where roots chase moisture deep underground and fruit ripens intensely sweet, concentrated, and low in water content. Give it lean, extremely well-drained soil and withhold supplemental water once plants are established, since irrigation dilutes the characteristic flavor that makes this tomato prized for the fried tomato fritters (tomatokeftedes) of Cycladic cooking. Harvest in small clusters as fruit turns deep red, and expect a sprawling, somewhat untidy plant habit typical of island landraces grown for flavor rather than uniformity.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

planting.note: Direct sow in autumn once summer heat breaks, so the crop develops through the mild, rain-fed Cycladic winter and dries down before summer; this legume is not the broad bean (Vicia faba) despite the shared culinary name.

directions: Santorini fava is a small-seeded legume landrace, distinct from the broad bean despite sharing its common Greek name, grown on the island's volcanic soil without irrigation and holding European PDO protection. Sow thickly in well-drained ground in autumn and let the crop grow through winter rains with no supplemental water, since the plant's deep taproot is adapted to the island's dry farming tradition. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before threshing, then simmer the small yellow-brown seeds into the creamy pureed dish, also called fava, that gives the crop its name. The lean volcanic soil and minimal irrigation are credited with the seed's fast-cooking texture and mild, slightly sweet flavor compared to related legumes grown in richer ground.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

common_name: Florina Pepper (Piperia Florinas, Greek Roasting Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm; Florina peppers need a long, warm season for the elongated fruit to ripen fully to red.

directions: Florina pepper is a long, tapering, thin-walled sweet pepper grown around the Macedonian town of Florina in northern Greece, where it carries European PDO status and is the pepper of choice for the roasted, oil-and-vinegar pepper salads served across the region. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with a stake or cage to support heavily laden branches, and harvest once fruit has turned from green to a deep glossy red for the sweetest flavor and easiest peeling after roasting. Char the thin-fleshed pods whole over flame or under a broiler, then peel and marinate in olive oil, garlic, and vinegar in the traditional Macedonian style. Pick successively through the season to keep plants setting new fruit.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

planting.note: Direct sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis after the last frost; this vigorous runner bean needs the full season and cool nights common at its native highland elevation to size up its outsized seed.

directions: Gigantes Kastorias is a runner bean landrace grown in the cool highland basin around Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in northwestern Greece, prized for producing some of the largest dry bean seeds in cultivation and holding European PDO status. Provide a tall trellis for the vigorous climbing vines, which, like other runner beans, set pods most reliably where summer nights stay cool rather than scorching hot. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the broad, flat, cream-colored seeds, then slow-bake them with tomato, olive oil, and herbs in the classic Greek gigantes plaki. Store dried seed in a sealed container out of light to preserve its creamy texture.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

planting.note: Plant seed tubers as soon as soil can be worked in spring; growers on Naxos take advantage of the island's fertile plain and spring rains to grow the crop without irrigation until tubers bulk up.

directions: Naxos potato is grown on the fertile central plain of the Cycladic island of Naxos, the only island in the group with enough fresh water and arable soil to support a significant potato crop, and it holds European PDO status. Plant seed tubers in well-drained, moderately fertile ground as soon as the soil can be worked, and hill soil around the stems as they grow to protect developing tubers from sun greening. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, curing tubers briefly in a shaded, airy spot before storage. The crop is known locally for a smooth, thin skin and firm, flavorful flesh well suited to roasting and the island's traditional potato dishes.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

common_name: Zante Currant Grape (Corinthian Currant, Black Corinth)

planting.note: Plant dormant, bare-root or potted vines in early spring against a trellis or wire system; this old Greek grape is naturally seedless and vigorous, needing an established support before it fruits heavily.

directions: Zante currant grape is the ancient seedless vine grown around Patras, Corinth, and the island of Zakynthos that gives dried Zante currants their name, long predating the unrelated black currant shrub despite the shared word. Train young vines onto a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and prune hard each winter, since this variety fruits on new wood and produces heavily once established. The tiny, intensely sweet purple-black berries ripen in dense clusters in late summer and are traditionally sun-dried on racks or trays into the small, dark dried fruit used across Mediterranean and British baking. Fresh clusters can also be eaten out of hand, offering a sugary, slightly tart flavor concentrated by the grape's small size.
sources: UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center

planting.note: Sow or transplant into lean, rocky, fast-draining ground in spring; this island population self-sows readily on volcanic slopes and tolerates salt spray, wind, and near-total summer drought once established.

directions: Santorini's wild caper population is harvested for both its pickled flower buds and its young leaves, a dual use that distinguishes the local kapari tradition from most other Mediterranean caper regions, which pickle buds alone. Grow in extremely lean, sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil and avoid any supplemental feeding, since rich conditions produce rank, less flavorful growth compared to the plant's native volcanic hillsides. Once established, the sprawling shrub needs essentially no irrigation and tolerates salt spray, wind, and reflected heat that would damage most other herbs. Harvest the smallest unopened buds and tender young leaf tips in late spring, then cure both in a dry salt brine before a final vinegar or brine pack, the traditional preparation that gives Santorini kapari its distinctive sharp, tangy bite.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost once soil has warmed; give the sprawling or trellised vines room to run, and harvest young and often for the mildest flavor.

directions: Katsouni is a traditional Cretan landrace botanically classed with melons rather than true cucumbers, yet grown and eaten exactly like a cucumber, picked young and pale green before the fruit's latent melon sweetness develops. Train the rampant vines onto a trellis or fence to keep the long, slightly ribbed fruit straight and easy to harvest, and pick every few days once fruiting begins to prevent oversized, seedy specimens. The thin skin and crisp, mild flesh make it a favorite sliced raw in Cretan salads with olive oil, oregano, and feta. Leave a few fruit to mature fully on the vine each season if saving seed, since overripe specimens shift toward true melon flavor and texture.
